doc.title: Red Holloway interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

chapter: Army, Chicago clubs and Joe Williams
title: Club DeLisa, Joe Williams, and Lloyd Price's band with James Brown and Ray Charles
summary: He recalls meeting Joe Williams at Club DeLisa, its floor shows, Red Saunders, and the all-night jam sessions and breakfast dances. He also recalls Lloyd Price's big band and that the blues is always boss.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Can you tell us anything about your work with Joe Williams?

Yeah, you know like I met Joe way back, in fact I wish I had thought about it. There is a clipping I could have brought from Club DeLisa in Chicago. And it was Joe Williams “Stop Pretty Baby, Stop,” that song that he did. It’s a little clipping from Club DeLisa. I was working with, what was her name, Little Miss Cornshucks, I was working at the Club DeLisa with her. And there was just a whole, just a whole advertisement of Joe Williams and with whom he was working, you know, Red Saunders and so, but like I met him way back years ago in Chicago, and he was gigging, like we all would work, we’d do our regular gig during the week, then on Monday morning they would have what you call a Breakfast Dance. Every club would have, like Club DeLisa, from it would go all night Sunday night and they would have a Breakfast Dance from, it would start at 6:00 and go until 8:00. Anybody that was playing anywhere in Chicago, I mean all musicians. This place held a thousand people. It was called Club DeLisa. Red Saunders has been there for about 30 years. And Joe Williams worked there for quite a few years. Billy Eckstine, a lot of your name entertainers worked at this club cause they had chorus girls, they had eight chorus girls, they had a nine piece band, and they had comedians, I mean these were real shows. You don’t get real shows today. You get one singer after another. But like you had tap dancers, you had comedians, you had novelty acts, Butter Beans and Suzie, and Peg Leg Bates, you had a real collection of people to make up a show. The show would run maybe an hour and a half you know. But then when they would finish, when they would finish then the band would play for half an hour, and people would dance, you know the stage would go up for the show and when the show was over the stage would come down and people would go and dance. I mean it was a big affair, and the place would be jam packed every Monday morning. Then when you left the Club DeLisa, you would go to other clubs and the jam sessions would start Monday morning until the next

morning about 5 AM Tuesday morning. I mean and I mean every club had something happening. You know so what would happen, I used to see Joe, he might be working at DeLisa and then he would probably go over to maybe over on 39th Street or to the Dusable Hotel or some of those different places and maybe do a gig or something. And you’d always, everybody would meet up at a certain place and have breakfast, and during those days the popular food was brains and eggs. Of course I know you wouldn’t think of that today. But you’d go have brains and eggs and biscuits and stuff like that and you’d hang out and talk stuff all morning. So Chicago really was, I mean like Dexter Gordon and Sonny Stitt and Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie — everybody would be in town. You would have the Dorsey Brothers and Harry James, but everyone would come to this particular club. So that’s what I have, this club with Joe on it. And there were a few occasions where we would run across each other, because I’d work the Regal Theater which was the theater that had all the different shows, you know, and like Count Basie’s band would come there and Duke Ellington, and they would still have a complete stage show with comedians and dancers and stuff. And Joe worked a lot of these different — So you know in your course of your playing this place to the other, you’d be playing with him, and I met him years ago. Yeah. He was light enough to ride a duck. But you know one of the things he always had a different type of voice than most vocalists. I mean his voice, his range was such, he had such a great range for his voice, that he could practically sing anything — opera as well as ballads. But of course now you know in America, the blues is always boss. I don’t care, you know it was so funny when I used to work with Lloyd Price, the band would play, he had like a 14 piece band. Now James Brown had a seven piece band, Ray Charles had an 8 or 9 piece band, and I used to work with Lloyd Price and we would play at Small’s Paradise in New York. So Lloyd Price would have James Brown as his guest, and then he’d have Ray Charles as his guest, but when both of them heard Lloyd’s band, you know, like the band would start playing but we wouldn’t be playing no blues to start off, we’d be playing some hip arrangements of whatever was popular for the day. And so when we were finished playing, and everybody had played their solos, and played like mad, the audience would say, “All right, now can y’all play us some blues?” So I’m just saying, blues is the boss. But when I mention a James Brown and Ray Charles, when they heard the band and heard what we played behind Lloyd Price, that’s when they decided — this was way back in the ‘60s, they said, “I’ve got to have me a band, got to have me a band, can’t have this seven piece.” And Ray Charles sounded good with his little small group, but he sounded better with a big band. So they all decided to have a band. But no matter what you play, the blues is always the boss. I’m sorry to say but it’s the truth.
